Ongoing and planned tau experiments require new theoretical calculations, particularly for decay processes involving virtual particles and complex reactions.

A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to cyclogenesis, namely the influence of rotation and temperature variations, in a simple yet comprehensive arrangement. The laboratory model enables researchers to control and analyze the formation of baroclinic waves through adjustments in temperature gradients and rotational rates, thereby creating distinctive wave patterns at the free surface of the rotating liquid. These experiments were conducted alongside numerical simulations by five groups using different methods and codes, with the goal of comparing theoretical and practical predictions of the wave patterns. While the simulations largely agreed with each other, the respective strengths and weaknesses of the models led to varying results. The numerical predictions were then validated against the corresponding experimental findings, with the aim of assessing the accuracy of the different methods in reproducing the complex dynamics of baroclinic waves.

A common strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences within a period to be part of a Poisson process. Yet the classic method based on this assumption has significant limitations, including the non-parametric nature of its parameters and issues related to unidentifiable parameters, particularly in cases with sparse data. This paper presents an alternative approach, which involves transforming the Poisson process rate parameter using a spectral method based on the generalized Ising model. The proposed reparameterization makes the parameter identifiable and easy to identify as well. The results show that this new approach efficiently captures both the relative intensity of occurrences and the time between them within an interval. The method is particularly effective at estimating the parameters for models of minimal and maximal extreme values. The findings also suggest that the new approach outperforms the standard method in terms of Bayesian model selection. Ultimately, this study provides a practical tool for analyzing and understanding extreme events, which has numerous applications in science and engineering.

In many real-world reinforcement learning applications, being able to adapt to the most effective policy after data collection is complete is crucial, a scenario known as offline reinforcement learning.  Offline RL faces a significant challenge when dealing with data integrity - its reliability relies heavily on the quality of the provided data-set.  When the data-set is compromised by an adversary, who manipulates the rewards, states, and actions within it, the offline RL solution may produce a policy that benefits the attacker rather than the learner.  This raises a safety concern that can be mitigated by developing an offline RL solution with an added layer of security - one that yields a policy beneficial to the learner, even when the data-set has been corrupted by an adversary with limited means.  This paper introduces a security framework and provides a specific solution in which the adversary's control is limited to altering a portion of the data-set's samples - their actions, states, and rewards.  To achieve this, the researchers presented a new approach, at the heart of which is a security guarantee, known as corruption-resilience, which can be computed by analyzing the effectiveness of the policy in the worst-case scenario of corrupted data.  Additionally, the researchers provided a specific approach, at its core is sample splitting - dividing the data into a clean set for training a model and an augmented set for learning an action-value function.  The effectiveness of this approach was validated through experiments conducted on a grid world environment and a classic game - Tic-Tac

This study demonstrates a practical application of a recent result in convex analysis to establish the logarithmic concavity of solutions to the 1-D heat equation, under dynamic boundary conditions that are sublinear in space and time. This approach facilitates the proof of impulsive controllability for this type of equation with the same boundary conditions, using a variable impulsive control of minimal amplitude supported on a relatively small interval in time.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We analyzed this issue by examining various approaches to detect pseudo-OOD and real-OOD texts within a language model's training domain, identifying two distinct forms of OOD examples - those that are linguistically similar (semantically OOD) and those that are not. Our analysis indicates that detecting both forms of OOD examples is crucial for minimizing model errors. Our study also explores how to develop multiple OOD detection methods in conjunction with data labeling, different model types, and data processing techniques. The use of these techniques was found to significantly improve the model's overall accuracy in identifying OOD examples.

In recent years, self-assembled nanoachines have been gaining attention due to their potential to create novel nanoscale devices. Among the various methods to activate them, using inelastic electron tunneling stands out as a means to induce dynamical movement. A theoretical model has been devised to simulate and analyze the movement of Brownian molecular engines powered by inelastic electron tunneling. The model considers the engine's circular base and the tunneling current coming from a metal island, as well as the influence of orbital degrees of freedom on the tunneling process. The model can predict the distribution of the engine's radius and its rotation speed, which can be compared to experimental results. The analysis can also identify key factors that affect the engine's movement, such as the tunneling current's strength and the level of friction. By adjusting these factors, the probability distribution of the engine's radius can be refined, matching experimental results. The model's findings can provide guidance for the design and optimization of molecular machines driven by inelastic electron tunneling.

We introduce a version of transducer resynchronizability that applies in one direction, by building upon previously established criteria for two-way resynchronization. These criteria include the extended Parp-Schaffer-Gillilhan criterion, the Brzozowski-Jankowski criterion, and the Charlier-Lalire criterion. Each of these criteria will be referred to as the BJS criterion for simplicity.

In this research, we investigate speeding up the calculation of generalized convolutions, specifically $f(g)(x)$, where $f$ and $g$ are functions, by leveraging recent breakthroughs in fast Fourier transform (FFT) algorithms for multivariate polynomial evaluations and divisions. We demonstrate the extension of these applications to calculate generalized convolutions through the application of a new operator, $\mathcal{G}$, which allows us to express $f(g)(x)$ as $f \circ \mathcal{G}(g)(x)$. This new operator is shown to have unique properties when applied to specific function spaces, including spaces of Lagrange interpolations, and can be represented as a Fourier transform followed by a element-wise operation. These properties enable the efficient computation of $f(g)(x)$ for certain function spaces through the use of FFT. Additionally, we propose a new method for calculating the inverse of a Toeplitz matrix, particularly for entry-wise scaled circulant matrices, by applying an inverse FFT like approach, which leverages the explicit inverse of the matrix's generating vector. This research also leads to a new method for calculating the convolution sum, $f(g)(x)$, for certain function spaces, which can be done more efficiently using FFT.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 sparked significant debate about its formation. Recent studies by the APOLLO project employed a machine learning-based approach to re-analyze spectra from various telescopes, yielding accurate temperature and luminosity estimates for GJ 229B. Our analysis reveals a temperature-range of 651 to 1000 K by machine learning, which coincides with previous findings. However, the precise nature of GJ 229B's mass and composition remains unclear despite the detailed spectral analysis. By assuming the dwarf is composed of iron-cobalt rocks with a typical human composition, the analysis estimates a mass range of 11 to 41 Earth masses for GJ 229B. Our work demonstrates the capability of the APOLLO project to provide reliable constraints on the characteristics of extra-solar planets using a fully automated approach.

To search for the potential existence of the $0^{--}$ state, we created a system of $u\dbar u\dbar u$ within a large box of 12 fm, then applied an orthogonal basis to the $0^{--}$ state, and calculated the partial wave projections of the $u\dbar u\dbar u$ system. Our results from the partial wave projections, denoted as $K_{\Lambda \Phi}^{J^P}(L^P)$, show that around 1% of the $u\dbar u\dbar u$ system has a $0^{--}$ component. We used the $T$-transform method to disentangle the $0^-$ and $0^{++}$ components from the $0^{--}$ component and found that about 0.3% of the $u\dbar u\dbar u$ system has a pure $0^{--}$ component. We also found that the $0^{--}$ component is concentrated below 1 GeV, which suggests that the $0^{--}$ state may contribute to the phenomenon observed at BESIII. Our study provides a theoretical foundation for the search of the $0^{--}$ state in experimental studies.

This contribution to the 10th Conference of the Asia Pacific School and Conference on Algebraic Geometry and its Applications (APSAG 2019) outlines the current status of the $\phi_s$-sideband subtraction technique used for evaluating the $\bar{B}^0_s$ meson decay width $\Delta\Gamma_s$. It also discusses the role of $\Delta\Gamma_s$ measurements in testing the Standard Model and the methodology for its determination with $B^0_s \to j/\psi X$ decays at LHCb.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is quantified using a dynamic model that assumes turbulent air mixing. The model calculates the infection risk based on the position of an infected passenger relative to other passengers and the efficiency of viral emission. These factors are incorporated into a Monte Carlo simulation that estimates the probability of transmission. Our model confirms that of Tai et al. (2020) and suggests that passengers seated directly opposite an infected person are about 8.12 times more likely to contract the disease than those seated further away. Our analysis extends to considering the distance between passengers, assuming varying degrees of air mixing and using different emission rates, and exploring the impact of these factors on transmission probability.

This study has conducted large-scale shell-model computations for $\beta$-decay attributes. Researchers at ILL, Grenoble, recently performed $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy to investigate $\beta$-decay properties of $^{137}$Te. Our calculations employed the ADMA Monte Carlo sampling method and explored the nuclear structure of even-even, odd-odd, and odd-proton and odd-neutron partners to $^{135,137}$Te using the SD-polarized Monte Carlo sampling method and GNOM matrix in which the $dp$-space is truncated to 12. Our findings include calculated $\beta$-$\beta$ decay properties of $^{135}$Te, in addition to $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy outcomes for $^{137}$Te. Our $^{135}$Te-related data include the $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy, nuclear wave functions, and electron-capture probabilities, along with the calculated $\beta$-$\beta$ decay properties of $^{135}$Te. Our results from $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy for $^{137}$Te consist of the transition scheme, transition strengths, and calculated log$~f$-values.

Double Sided Auctions are versatile and widely applicable negotiation protocols that are often used in modeling and simulating market interactions. They suit situations where multiple buyers and sellers exchange a single commodity, making them suitable for tasks like price prediction and market simulation. This protocol has been used in various contexts, but our investigation reveals that the standard implementation has a significant drawback - it can result in erroneous prices and unproductive negotiations. We have developed a refined version of the protocol that addresses these issues, creating what we term 'Validated Double Sided Auctions'. This improved auction ensures that the resulting price is fair to all participants and achieves a satisfactory trade for everyone involved. To justify our protocol, we develop a formal definition of market mechanisms and establish a key property regarding their validity.

The properties of F-wave bottom mesons, specifically their transition form factors, are investigated using heavy quark effective theory and a light-front quark model. The study aims to gain insight into how these form factors change with energy as well as test the reliability of the light-front quark model for this type of calculation. The results are also compared with an existing calculation using a different method in the standard perturbative framework.

In the context of nonexpansive functions, an important aspect is to understand periodic points and the trajectories connecting them, especially since this class of functions includes projections onto convex sets and thus has significant implications in convex optimization. Researchers have shown that any nonexpansive function defined on a finite collection of points in a Euclidean space can be expressed as a finite sum of periodic functions with indices that are also periodic. By leveraging this periodic decomposition, the paper demonstrates that the nonexpansive function can be expressed as a finite sum of convex functions defined on periodic intervals. Additionally, the paper identifies a specific class of nonexpansive functions that are periodic and have a unique fixed point, and it proves that the trajectories of these functions are continuous and invertible. Furthermore, the paper presents a geometric interpretation of these results, demonstrating that the ball mapping associated with any nonexpansive function defined on a finite collection of points in a Euclidean space can be expressed as a finite sum of periodic functions with indices that are also periodic.

We introduce a new method for determining the parameters of a Gaussian process kernel used in the Dynamic Mode Decomposition algorithm via optimization. This kernel, central to the algorithm, generates a matrix that informs the algorithm's decomposition process. Our method employs an optimization framework to select the kernel parameter, which we call the Kernel Learning Dynamic Mode Decomposition (KLDMD) algorithm. Through simulations, we demonstrate that the kernel can be optimized to reduce errors in the resulting equations for the invariants of interest. Notably, our approach allows for nonlinear optimization, broadening the applicability of Dynamic Mode Decomposition. Additionally, we have found that optimizing the kernel can significantly reduce errors associated with modeling discrepancies, thereby providing more accurate results. Our method is open to various kernel types but is specifically illustrated with the squared exponential kernel. Our work addresses the challenge of choosing the kernel parameter, often done heuristically or by cross-validation, by developing a derivative-free optimization framework that yields improved results.

The timeless appeal of chess persists, with its strategic complexities still captivating players across the globe, particularly when it comes to mastering the intricacies of opening gameplay which separates novices from experienced players. Using a vast dataset from the online chess forum ChessTempo, which boasts over 1 million registered players and a comprehensive database of chess strategies, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the intricacy and similarity within chess openings. By employing a cluster analysis, which groups similar elements together based on their characteristics, we identified the most relevant aspects of closing techniques in chess and evaluated their levels of complexity. Our findings reveal that good players are distinguished from beginners by their mastery of basic opening strategies, while more advanced players are set apart by their proficiency in subtle variations. Additionally, our study shows that the most popular opening techniques, which are widely adopted by high-ranking players, are also the most efficient in terms of winning potential. These conclusions were further substantiated through an experimental study, which demonstrated that using more intricate opening strategies in blind chess games leads to improved outcomes. Ultimately, our research provides valuable insights for chess players on the most effective opening techniques, as well as their strategic benefits, by offering personalized recommendations tailored to players of varying skill levels.

This research explores the potential internal structures of neutron stars (NSs) and the mechanisms of their mass loss through gravitational wave emission. By utilizing the concept of annihilating iron in the interior of NSs within binary systems, researchers have estimated the mass and radius of these stars. This study extends such studies to pulsars in binary systems, specifically those classified as millisecond pulsars (MSPs). However, direct calculations based on observed data are complicated by uncertainties surrounding the initial mass of the progenitor star and the metal content of the star. Therefore, researchers devised an alternative approach to understand the internal structure of NSs in binary systems through radiation of gravitational waves. They applied this approach to a hypothetical star that undergoes no mass change throughout its evolution and considered a range of possible core-mass fractions during the therapeutic process. By calculating fundamental NS parameters based on different initial metal contents and considering the effects of external forces acting on the star, researchers derived a range of possible values for these parameters. Notably, calculations for a pale dwarf binary system resulted in an estimated radius of 12.7 to 13.8 kilometers for an NS with a mass of 1.17 to 1.28 solar masses. Researchers also computed various Love numbers for NSs in this binary system and identified potential constraints on which evolutionary pathways NSs must have experienced to explain their observed properties.

A theoretical framework to study Lagrangian dynamics beyond the first derivative is developed using a formulated theory. This framework generalizes the principle of least action and reveals a close relationship between conservation laws and differential identities derived from the Lagrangian. Based on this theoretical framework, a proof of the existence of conserved quantities in differential forms is provided for a class of Lagrangians. Furthermore, this proves a previously proposed conjecture regarding the conservation of forms. In addition, this framework is used to investigate a known problem in differential geometry involving the conservation of higher-order Lagrangians.

Our proposed technique enables users to retrieve three-dimensional shapes through virtual drawing. By leveraging deep learning and geometry, we generate a query shape that matches the user's sketching capabilities. The retrieval shape is derived from the sketch via a mapping function to both its surface and volume properties. The surface and volume components guide the shape retrieval, and as such, the system is capable of finding both similar three-dimensional models and applications (or categories) based on the user's creativity. For instance, drawing a cube indicates an interest in solid shapes, whereas a stylized sketch of a cube might indicate a fascination with art or design. By taking into account both volume and surface information, our system allows for retrieval not just of similar three-dimensional models but also of categories (or applications), such as geometric primitives, where a drawn cone may indicate an interest in spheres, and a stylized cone might suggest a fascination with design. The retrieval information can then be utilized for downstream tasks in graphics and design, spanning 3D printing of actual objects to generating computational models of data-driven 3D shapes.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, creates a notable albedo pattern in transit due to its thick atmosphere, making it suitable for studying the planet's properties using space telescopes like James Webb. To utilize these observations efficiently, it's crucial to schedule them at the points in the planet's highly eccentric orbit when it is closest to its star, as observed transits at other times may be affected by inaccurately predicted arrival times. Recent observations from the TEEE transits project, a global network of telescopes that monitor HD80606b's transits, have been combined with predictions from various sources to refine the planet's orbit. At approximately 18 days before periastron, when the planet is under the least influence from its parent star's light, a new transit was identified through photometry collected from multiple telescopes, allowing the periastron point to be marked at CNTRS (CTES) 2.728684 +/- 0.000011, which matches the findings from a 2019 analysis by a different group. To incorporate these results, the authors have developed a novel extrapolation technique based on a point-mass ephemeris model, as well as another based on a seven-term polynomial model that will be used for future transit scheduling until the next periastron at CNTRS (CTES) 2.728684.

In this investigation, we're looking at how matter behaves during a collapse in a spherically symmetric Isentropic environment, where the matter's pressure is directly tied to the density, and the initial conditions are determined experimentally. We find that in most cases, the matter's density keeps getting more concentrated, but there's always a chance it'll reach a point where the pressure becomes too weak to stop the collapse, and a black hole forms. If we simulate a range of mass loss during the collapse, we can figure out how different types of matter behave and see if the end result depends on the collapse starting with either a bounce or a singularity. We discover that in most cases, the manner in which the matter behaves during the collapse doesn't change based on the collapse itself, and we explain this phenomenon using properties of the potential energy in such environments.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the radiation emitted by extreme black holes. This method has been effectively applied to calculate corrections for Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordstrom, and de Sitter spacetimes. Additionally, we have derived formulas for correcting the Hawking radiation, and our approach can likely be extended to other extreme black holes.

A key consideration in motor skill development is understanding the purpose behind practice-driven improvements in movement outcomes. We investigated this by linking outcome metrics to a model of the central nervous system's prediction processing, which explains the connection between practice-driven movements and perceived consequences. The study's results revealed that simply predicting the movement trajectory, without considering the movement's final state, is insufficient to explain the outcome of motor training. On the other hand, incorporating the movement's ending point into prediction processing aligns with observations of motor learning progress. The incorporation of end-effect considerations in motor training scenarios offers new, useful insights.

A new approach is introduced to develop non-perturbative, causal actions for gravity and a charged point particle moving in a background field, emphasizing a precise duality between the particle action and a key operator from the Poincaré algebra. This method yields a novel, symmetric form for the particle action. When the background field is reduced to a gauge potential, the action develops a symmetry equivalent to the Poincaré algebra. Utilizing a non-perturbative variational method allows us to directly obtain the equations of motion for both the particle and gravity actions. In the case of the charged particle action, a key operator from the algebra provides the conservative form of the Hamiltonian. This approach also leads to a new, innovative form of the relativistic Lagrangian for a charged particle.

Upward planarity, a concept where a graph's embedding can be represented with arrows pointing upwards, has seen significant advancements in parameterized algorithms over the past decade. Recent discoveries regarding bounded treewidth structures and graphs with low vertex degree have led to the development of faster, more efficient algorithms for upward planarity. Specifically, a parameterized algorithm for bounded treewidth structures with O(4.22k) time complexity and linear vertex degree graphs with O(2.01k) time complexity have been achieved. The time complexity for linear vertex degree graphs has been a long-standing open question, and these advancements provide considerable reductions to O(2k) time. The new findings offer promising applications, particularly in modeling various real-world scenarios through treewidth structures and linear vertex degree graphs. The research may potentially enable the efficient visualization of up to k-layer networks, depending on their composition.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but lack a unified framework to assess their effectiveness.
We propose the MemoNav challenge, introducing a comprehensive evaluation framework to examine the role of memory in visual navigation, comparing existing approaches to their strengths and weaknesses.
Our analysis reveals that current methods fall short in their generalization to new environments and scenarios, and we address this by developing a new method that integrates multiple memory sources and adapts to unseen settings through adaptative memory selection.
The MemoNav challenge will serve as a research benchmark to investigate the importance of memory in visual navigation, facilitating further research and analysis.

To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells (Femto Cells) by reusing the same licensed spectrum. However, these cells' capabilities were insufficient to support future applications like virtual reality and augmented reality. As a result, operators have sought to deploy 4G LTE small cells in unlicensed spectrum, primarily in the 5 GHz Wi-Fi band. Although these cells have successfully addressed the capacity issue in areas with high data demand, they have not fully resolved the issue of excessive interference in unlicensed spectrum. To tackle this problem, this paper examines the development and deployment of 4G LTE small cells and looks to the future, discussing the present and future of small cell technology in the context of 6G.

This overview covers the underlying complex relationships between the interconnected systems and the complex behaviors that arise from their interactions, specifically looking at complex systems from a dynamical systems perspective. 

To better understand and analyze these interactions, our approach utilizes a comprehensive framework that combines network topology and dynamics, enabling the identification of universal patterns in intricate systems. 

Through examination of various examples, such as interdependent networks in electricity and transportation, as well as network dynamics in biology and brain function, we observe that disruption to one part of these complex systems can have far-reaching effects on others. 

As a result, maintaining global stability requires balancing competition for resources to maintain overall system resilience. 

Ultimately, our work highlights the need for multi-faceted approaches to manage and understand these intricate connections.

We examine the relationship between operator growth and the hierarchy of operators within the context of CFTs, specifically focusing on cases where the operator product expansion (OPE) hierarchies closely resemble one another. Our analysis reveals that similarities in these hierarchies are sufficient for determining a linear relationship between the dimensions of corresponding operators. We further establish that in OPE hierarchies, the appearance of lower-dimensional operators is sufficient to predict the dimension of the primary operators, and identify a specific pattern in the hierarchy structure that enables this prediction to occur. To reinforce our findings, we provide concrete examples of OPE hierarchies with intricate properties.

Researchers have provided new insights into the structure of the elusive Hoyle state, a state that has garnered significant interest due to its unique properties. The Hoyle state, composed of six particles, is thought to exist across various nuclei and is characterized by its robust, compact structure. The presence of the Hoyle state as a distinct resonance has been supported by multiple studies, but its theoretical foundations remain unclear. The 16-O nucleus, of particular interest to scientists, exhibits a complex decay pattern that is difficult to interpret using established theoretical models. The goal of a recent experiment was to measure the direct decay of the Hoyle state into three alpha particles and a 12-C nucleus using the TPC camera at J-PET to understand its properties. The analysis of the experiment's data revealed a significant component of the Hoyle state's decay, a finding that is consistent with previous studies. The ratio of the natural widths between the Hoyle state and its 0.20 MeV higher-energy counterpart, the 5.65 MeV state, was also determined to be approximately 0.70, a value that is in line with earlier measurements. The gamma-ray energy spectrum near 5.65 MeV, dominated by finite geometric effects, showed a modest component that is thought to be the direct decay of the Hoyle state. The observed gamma rays, traveling long distances through the J-PET detector, were found to be influenced by scattering events, a phenomenon that is thought to account for a significant

Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of a threshold for the fracture instability parameter, independent of material and fracture characteristics in brittle solids. The scaling theory for fracture instability has been further developed by incorporating a new length scale, quantifying viscoelastic effects in time and space. The modified theory is then used to simulate fracture patterns through a simple, explicit rule. The simulated results show a strong correlation with numerical simulations based on viscoelastic energy balance equations. The proposed theory and length scale are not only applicable to regular crack surfaces but also extend to irregular surfaces, capturing the essence of fracture instability in solids.

We explore the capacity and optimal power allocation in a specific class of feedback channels, where the transmitter has access to accurate past received information. This is equivalent to studying a discrete memoryless channel that maintains its past received data, with the sender having access to this information via a confidential, binary communication channel. Our study establishes a critical relationship between the conditional entropy of the source given the past received data and a binary noise channel, along with finding a general bound for the mutual information between the source and the state of the channel. This investigation is further extended to find the maximum achievable mutual information subject to a given power constraint, with the effect of feedback being quantified in terms of a tight bound. This model is analogous to a specific situation in a channel with memory, where the sender has access to the past received data, resulting in a lower bound on the mutual information in this case. The proposed approach is a iterative convex optimization algorithm, which is found to be tight and efficient, with the capacity of this feedback channel being fully achieved. Additionally, this method is also applied to find the optimal power allocation in a general setting with feedback.

In a theoretical study, researchers investigated the existence of topological superfluidity in an attractive Rashba-harmonized hydrogen-like atom, where they observed spin-singlet paired-dense states and found that the associated superfluidity exhibits topological properties. Additionally, within a weak coupling regime, the system shows similarity with the properties of polonium-210. Further analysis revealed that the structure of the system's energy spectrum near its ground state consists of an infinite sequence of distinct, non-degenerate states separated by a gap in energy, where the largest gap occurs at the boundary. This topological superfluidity is stabilized by applying an effective magnetic field within a thin, two-dimensional ring-shaped confining potential where the width of the band, determined by the magnetic field strength, is a key factor in deciding the existence of the system's topological superfluidity. It's noted that the associated edge modes conferring the system's non-topological characteristics possess measurable energy and can be stabilized through applied magnetic fields. Furthermore, the observed Rashba effect in superfluidity arises from the inclusion of spin-orbit coupling, where it either produces topological superfluidity or prevents it, respectively. This finding represents the first reported occurrence of Rashba effect in superfluidity.

This study focuses on understanding the extraction of factual information from scientific documents, particularly tables, through the application of natural language processing techniques. To address this challenge, we introduced a new dataset for SemEval 2021 Task 9: SEM-TAB-Facts, requiring participants to engage in two related activities. Firstly, they had to verify whether individual table cells contained accurate information by comparing data to a established reference set. Secondly, they had to locate supporting evidence within the original scientific documents, also organized into a reference set. Two subtasks were involved in this process: verifying whether table cells contained factual information, and identifying relevant evidence in the documents, both presented in a tabular format. To measure performance, we used a combination of metric, heuristics-based evaluation for cell accuracy and evidence finding, submitted by 25 teams in total, and received excellent feedback with multiple top-performing teams.

This analysis builds upon my previous paper 'The Nature of Numbers in Quantum Mechanics' and explores the potential benefits of utilizing complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics. In the referenced paper, I argued that complex numbers are not inherently necessary for Quantum mechanics, as a real-valued formulation can effectively describe the theory. However, this present work focuses on the advantages of complex numbers within the context of Quantum mechanics. It is found that complex numbers facilitate the representation of quantum states through hyperbolic geometry, enabling a more intuitive and visually appealing analysis of measurement outcomes and wave function evolution. Moreover, utilizing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics is found to be linked to the widespread application of complex analysis in describing physical phenomena. Finally, this work examines the potential for complex numbers to be substituted with more general number systems, specifically the number sets used in Lorentzian geometry and Cantor space, with a focus on their implications for Quantum mechanics.

This research introduces a modified version of the metric dimension concept, termed "trimmed metric dimension", and investigates its associated problems. Theoretical analyses are provided to establish the feasibility of determining minimum trimmed metric dimensions in graphs, along with a related NP-hardness proof for general graphs. A algorithm is proposed to compute the minimum trimmed metric dimension of a graph with diameter two.

These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By "distant," I'm referring to ground levels where Darcy's law remains largely unaltered due to the transverse hydraulic head being negligible. These equations help streamline numerical models of groundwater flow by limiting computational domains to the near-surface region. 

To establish these equations, I employed a singular perturbation method with the far-field boundary conditions integral to the result. These conditions are in line with traditional approaches but require adjustment when considering long-distance flows. 

For confidence in my approach, I compared the calculated steady-state water table behavior with established analytical solutions. Additionally, I considered unconfined and confined groundwater systems together with verifying that when distances become sufficiently close, these equations align with full three-dimensional Darcy's law. 

These equations were also applied in a conjugate gradient method solving a transient case of unconfined groundwater flow.

This work has investigated the potential of integrating an ozone O3 and ultraviolet (UV) light system for effectively eliminating pollutants in flue gas emissions. A numerical model of a continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) was used to simulate and analyze the removal of sulfur dioxide SO2 through gas-phase oxidation. Various UV radiation models were considered, each involving a grid convergence study to determine the optimal number of discrete light sources for maximum performance. The simulated reactions were validated against available literature data, and the resulting model was used to investigate alternative configurations of UV-O3 systems to meet 99% removal efficiency standards for SO2 while minimizing energy consumption and costs.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in testing and evaluating the efficacy of their designs in real-world applications. To address this issue, we have developed a modular, portable simulation environment utilizing SystemC, allowing for the development of transaction-level models for neuromorphic systems. This versatile framework is designed to support multiple hardware architectures, such as FPGA-based and custom silicon designs, and can be easily adapted for new configurations. We have successfully implemented a virtual platform for the BrainSimples CM1b board, which is an open-source platform for testing neural network applications. This simulation platform can serve as a useful tool for evaluating and refining neuromorphic computing architectures in education and research environments.

Many machine learning tasks are adapted from established models or solved with established methods, but this study targets situations with three key complexities: structures with multiple interconnected parts, and relationships based on quantities with no clear boundaries, relationships that can be restricted, and relationships that can overlap. We identify which common machine learning approaches are insufficient for these situations and introduce a new framework, Indecision Forests, which is based on a type of argument-based reasoning commonly used in law and allows for the representation of complex relationships through trees, with every change affecting many branches, and for the representation of boundaries through trees, with areas classified as uncertain. Since there is no obvious direct approach, we frame this task as a learning problem and test various approaches, modifying them to fit this new framework, while also evaluating the inherent challenges.

The DTW distance is commonly employed in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and similarity search tasks, but its time complexity hinders its efficiency in large-scale similarity searches. To overcome this, some strategies involve precomputing and storing DTW distances for all time series in a database, then discarding irrelevant results early in the retrieval process. A more efficient approach, PrunedDTW, achieves better performance by eliminating unnecessary database time series considerations during a single pass through the data. A faster variant, EDP PrunedDTW or EDPD, provides even better performance by reducing the bound calculations, though at the cost of less accurate prediction and increased error in advance discarding predictions. A recent study found that EDPD outperforms PrunedDTW in most cases, but two specific scenarios involve EDPD's error causing it to perform worse: when the median DTW distance is low and when there is little time difference between the query and data sets. In response, researchers introduced early discarding variants of PrunedDTW, including EDP PrunedDTW, that can tell when EDPD's error will occur and switch to PrinedDTW instead, thus ensuring EDP PrunedDTW's performance surpasses that of EDPD and PrunedDTW. A key challenge in developing such early discarding variants involves determining when the margin for error in EDP PrunedDTW is too large, causing it to switch to PrunedDTW and

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or focus on teaching the structure and concepts of test cases, although not the actual code. To address the lack of educational tools that effectively combine concept assessment with testing education, we designed an inquiry-based testing tool that rewards students for writing well-structured test cases based on object-oriented principles. To empirically evaluate the effectiveness of this tool, we conducted an experiment involving 82 students from a university testing course and compared its outcomes with those of another tool, FeedbackPro. The experiment revealed that students using our tool demonstrated improved concept awareness and even performed similarly in terms of code coverage when compared to students using FeedbackPro. The tool's effectiveness was further validated through comments from instructors and students, who praised its ability to educate and its compatibility with existing teaching methods.

In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to cover the entire input space, offer no guarantee of being interpretable, or only provide partial explanations. This paper introduces a new approach that integrates the evaluation of feature importance with the use of interpretability to address these issues in explaining complex, deep neural network models. A key component of this method utilizes concept analysis to increase the scope of coverage, especially in situations where there are limited numbers of instances available for evaluation. This approach is demonstrated on both synthetic data and actual medical image datasets, specifically for the identification of tumors in lung CT scans.

Over-smoothing is a phenomenon where Graph Convolutional Networks fail to improve accuracy beyond a certain point by over-smoothing features, making them unusable. In this study, we explored the Graph Multi-Modal Convolutional Network, which combines graph convolutional networks with vision and message passing networks to address the over-smoothing issue. We developed an index to measure the over-smoothing effect and conducted experiments on four datasets. Our results show that Graph Multi-Modal Convolutional Networks can indeed defeat the over-smoothing issue, but the reliability of this improvement varies across different datasets and scenarios. We also analyzed the key components of our model to explain these observations.

A study focusing on the production of dark matter in association with a logically decaying Z boson is presented, using data collected by the CMS experiment at a 13 TeV proton-proton collision facility, totaling 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of accumulated data. By analyzing final states characterized by an Z boson decaying into a pair of electrons or muons, and an unknown dark matter particle, various model interpretations are explored. These models include the investigation of a mediator particle, dark photons, and a receptor-mediated theory, and the resulting data are consistent with standard model predictions across the entire phase space. Additionally, the study provides the most restrictive limits to date on the production of a 1 TeV dark particle through electroweak interaction, and also constraints a theory proposing the production of dark photons in 1 TeV dark matter events, both exceeding those expected from popular dark matter models.

We propose several symmetry-based distribution functions that depend on $k_\perp$ (transverse momentum), which are relevant to the study of high-energy hadron collisions and quark-gluon plasma. These functions, including a novel one, can be used to derive the previously established $x$-dependent Jettiness, $x$-and $k_\perp$-dependent Tails, and quasi-particle distribution functions. By establishing relationships between these functions, we resolve a longstanding uncertainty and explain why Jettiness and Tails are only sensitive to the $u$ and not the $d$ or $\bar{u}$ or $\bar{d}$ quark directions in certain contexts.

Homeomorphisms on compact, metrizable spaces with a specified topology can be given a topological structure by restricting to a specific type of convergence, which makes them a topological group.  When these spaces are given this restricted topology, they possess certain properties and can be given an equivalent topology if they have certain Homeomorphisms applied to them.  When the space is partitioned into two subsets with specific properties, its topological structure can be given an equivalent topology if both subsets have certain Homeomorphisms applied to them.  A specific type of convergence can also be given to the set of all Homeomorphisms on these spaces, which makes their homeomorphism classes form a topological group.  When these spaces are given this restricted topology, their homeomorphism group form a topological ring if and when the space is compact.  When the space is not metrizable but has a certain topological property, its topological structure can be given an equivalent topology if it satisfies a specific scaling condition, which makes its homeomorphism group form a topological ring.  A specific type of convergence can also be given to the set of all Homeomorphisms on these spaces, which makes their homeomorphism classes form a topological group.  When these spaces are given this restricted topology, their homeomorphism group form a topological group if and when the space is metrizable and has a certain topological property.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when the substrate was cleaned, Heusler film growth on graphene/disialin exhibited a unique, grain-bounding misorientation. We utilized density functional theory to analyze the chemistry behind the interface and found that contaminants from the sapphire substrate indeed react with graphene, but that interface also exhibits unique reactivity towards incoming remote epitaxial nuclei. This unexpected reactivity might explain previous findings of a grain-bounding epitaxial relationship in certain Heusler films grown on graphene. Our findings suggest that graphene can serve as a benign, reusable substitute for traditional single-crystal substrates in epitaxial remote epitaxy, but that the current cleaning protocols may be insufficient. With further optimization of the substrate cleaning process, the possibility of achieving true remote epitaxy using this technique could increase.

We analyze how to make reliable predictions in a group of individuals who have different levels of knowledge about their own distribution shapes. Assuming that the distributions of their data do not change over time, we use a method that combines their unique distribution shapes using a matrix called the Grammian. This matrix is comprised of quantities calculated from the individuals' data. Under specific assumptions, our method allows the sample size to be substantially smaller than the number of parameters being estimated. We verify the reliability of our method by conducting statistical tests. In simulations, we find that it outperforms other commonly used approaches. This research is demonstrated by data from people's perceptions of remote traffic noise.

Recent JWST observations of El Gordo, the massive galaxy cluster, have identified 23 known groups of multiply distorted galaxy images and 8 previously undiscovered ones, all verified spectroscopically by MUSE. By analyzing these groups, researchers created a new lens model which enabled the precise measurement of El Gordo's distance at approximately 0.81 billion light-years. This new model facilitated the detection of several distant and extremely large stars within these distorted galaxy images. One such star, identified as SRSB-234, is notable for being the first discovered of its kind outside of the Coma halo. Initial estimates suggest it is approximately 200 times brighter than the sun, with an estimated age of 1 billion years. JWST data also revealed multiple distinct populations within the cluster, each characterized by unique velocities. Further spectral analysis by MUSE revealed the presence of 32 population II and 8 population I galaxies within these distorted galaxy images, all verified spectroscopically. This new research significantly expands our understanding of the galactic distribution within the El Gordo cluster and provides an opportunity to study its historical development.

Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially towards maintaining and upgrading network infrastructure, especially with the rise of Network Neutrality debates. This paper proposes a novel, time-varying agreement that balances the competing interests of Content and Service Providers, with Content Providers compensating Service Providers for ensuring superior quality connections to their popular services. To arrive at this agreement, the paper employs a dynamic and reciprocal profit-sharing model, with both parties striving to maximize their respective profits. This co-opetitive model is further investigated through numerical analysis and case studies, demonstrating that Content Providers are willing to compensate Service Providers when there are usage disparities or varying content delivery demands over time.

The GNS construction forms a categorical functor that connects C*-algebras to a category of representation-carrying Hilbert spaces and representable *-homomorphisms, a specific type of morphism. In the context of weak C*-dilations, this construction serves as a constructive equivalent to the standard GNS construction, thereby enabling the reestablishment of the original C*-algebra and its faithful *-homomorphism through a categorical inversion. Similarly, in the case of Galois strong *-functors, the construction serves as a constructive equivalent to the standard GNS construction, allowing the reconstruction of the original *-functor through a categorical inversion.

The $\alpha$-attractor models, comprising of exponential potentials in a Lifshitz inflationary framework, have been shown to match observational values of primordial non-Gaussian features as well as predictions of the scalar spectral index from the simplest single-field models of inflation. We provide a comprehensive overview of these models, along with predictions for other inflationary parameters. We also offer a comparison with other single-field inflationary models, including those with pole-like potentials in a Lisfshitz scenario and flat potentials in an $F(R)$ gravity framework. Additionally, we examine to what extent the predictions of these models can be refined through the use of conformal perturbation theory.

In the context of a quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic three-dimensional manifold with a boundary that approaches infinity, its foliations measured at infinity directly relate to the horizontal measured foliations derived from the uniformization maps associated with its components that extend towards infinity. For a given hyperbolic surface that a pair of measured foliations, denoted by $\mathsf{F}_{+}$ and $\mathsf{F}_{-}$, completely fill, our analysis reveals that when sufficiently small, multiplying both $\mathsf{F}_{+}$ and $\mathsf{F}_{-}$ by a factor of $t>0$ results in unique isometries that preserve the surface. We then demonstrate that for a quasi-Fuchsian group that a hyperbolic surface is completely filled by a pair of measured foliations, its isometries measured at infinity, $\mathsf{F}_{+}^{\mathrm{inf}}$ and $\mathsf{F}_{-}^{\mathrm{inf}}$, remain unchanged under small changes. If the original group is deformed into a nearby Fuchsian group within the space of representations with bounded recurrence, the transformed measured foliations, denoted as $\mathsf{F}_{+}^{\mathrm{new}}$ and $\mathsf{F}_{-}^{\mathrm{new}}$, differ from $\mathsf{F}_{+}^{\mathrm{inf}}$ and $\mathsf{F}_{-}^

This study presents a unified framework for the cross-sectional distribution of fund returns and aims to address challenges associated with fund management, research, and investment decisions. It also opens up opportunities for around $4 trillion in assets under management to generate returns through a novel, proven approach. To this end, the paper addresses several critical questions: What are the fundamental drivers of fund performance? How do these factors impact performance? Which funds benefit from similar characteristics? How can a fund's historical performance be utilized to forecast its future returns? Ultimately, the study offers precise measurements of fund attributes and a precise model for forecasting fund performance.

Our research reveals that the primary factors driving fund returns are closely tied to the underlying characteristics of the funds themselves, rather than external market conditions or portfolio managers' decisions. This discovery has far-reaching implications for fund research, management practices, investment strategies, and regulatory policies.

By segmenting the fund universe based on shared characteristics, investors and regulators can gauge a fund's performance relative to its peers and make more informed decisions. This classification system also enables researchers to conduct more effective studies and informs investors about fund performance in order to make informed investment choices.

The study also provides a straightforward method for forecasting fund returns using historical performance data, addressing a long-standing challenge in the field. This model can be employed to evaluate a fund's performance, identify high-potential investment opportunities, and track changes in fund trends over time.

To demonstrate the practical value of our framework, the paper showcases various applications in fund

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation recordings is hampered by background noise and the recorder's effects on the signal.  To address this, this study investigates the effectiveness of machine learning classifiers when trained on recordings with varying types and levels of noise and interference.  Comparing signal enhancement methods with direct training on noisy signals, we find that the latter yields better results.  Additionally, we find that combining classifiers improves phonecreation identification but doesn't benefit nucleation identification.  To further challenge classification tasks, we introduce two new datasets: a larger dataset with recordings from multiple sources and another with recordings from patients undergoing surgery.  Our method holds potential for partial replacement of a healthcare professional's role in evaluating cardiac auscultation recordings.

In a 2021 study, we had developed a more accurate calculation for a specific nuclear transition in $^{133}$Cs using relativistic coupled-cluster theory. Recently, Roberts and Ginges raised concerns about a part of this calculation that they disagreed with, but it aligns with earlier calculations. In response, we clarify that the controversial aspect stems from different numerical methods used and not from any underlying theory. Additionally, we addressed concerns about possible systematic errors and found them to be negligible. Finally, we addressed a mistaken reference in the original paper.

This research examines various twist configurations applied to the torus, a circular and featureless surface, within a 2-dimensional crystallographic space. By combining visual and mathematical representations, our study showcases the diverse scenarios in which twists can occur, classified according to their symmetry patterns. Furthermore, we identify the underlying conditions necessary for twist configurations in terms of edge and vertex manipulations. Additionally, our investigation delves into the connection between twist patterns and the properties of fermionic and bosonic wave functions, using wave function symmetry as an essential diagnostic tool. Lastly, related concepts in condensed matter physics and topology are discussed, highlighting the intrinsic link between twist configurations and these advanced topics.

This analysis explores how internal characteristics within a group influence its ability to make decisions effectively, particularly in the context of responding to environmental challenges like climate change. Our research examines the impact of a token economy, which rewards virtuous behavior with points, and how the points are subsequently used to support climate-conscious projects in a laboratory setting. We compared the behavior of three types of groups: those with limited resources, those working together to address a common problem, and imaginary communities created to avoid the costs of cooperation. Our results show that in real-world groups, cooperation is greatest when members have a shared goal and resources are available to support it, and that rewarding positive behavior statistically significantly increases pro-social actions, although the effect is relatively small. We also discovered that groups with common goals and resources are more resilient to external stresses than fictive communities, which are essentially groups without a shared purpose or support structure. Our research has important implications for addressing climate change and promoting sustainable behavior within and between communities.

This research examines the properties of fractional integrals and derivatives within the context of discrete Hardy spaces, specifically $H^p($$\mathbb{Z}$, $\zeta$). We have derived novel means representations for the fractional integral of order $p>0$ and $\alpha>0$, as well as the fractional derivative of order $q>0$ and $\beta>0$ on the discrete Hardy space $H^p($$\mathbb{Z}$, $\zeta)$. We have further shown that the operator $I_f^{\alpha, \mathbb{Z}}$ is bounded from $H^p($$\mathbb{Z}$, $\zeta)$ to $H^p($$\mathbb{Z}$, $\zeta)$ for $p,\alpha\in (0,1]$ and that its inverse is given by $I^{\alpha, \mathbb{Z}^{-1}}$. We have also established that the operator $I_f^{(\alpha, \mathbb{Z})}$ is bounded from $H^p($$\mathbb{Z}$, $\zeta)$ to $H^p($$\mathbb{Z}$, $\zeta)$ for $p,\alpha\in (0,2]$ and that its inverse is given by $I_f^{(\mathbb{Z}, \alpha^{-1})}$. Moreover, we have derived some interesting consequences of these findings.

This study offers the first empirical evaluation of trust in private auctions, specifically examining trustworthiness in second-price auctions with a variety of sellers. Trust is measured as the likelihood that a buyer accepts a low bid from a known seller who has previously agreed on a higher price. Our results from repeated auctions with three sellers reveal that trust levels are highest when sellers are guaranteed to sell at a higher price and are subject to a penalty if they fail to meet this guarantee. However, even in this optimal scenario, trust levels are relatively low. We also discovered that trust levels are affected by sellers' ability to see the final auction price, with trust levels being higher when this information is accessible.

The explanation of accelerated cosmology through modified gravity theories has become a significant approach in theoretical cosmology, and one such theory is gravity that utilizes the teleparallel sector's symmetric part, denoted by $f(Q)$. Our research focuses on a specific subclass of locally rotationally symmetric Bianchi-I universes, where the goal is to determine which models remain compatible with observations and ultimate isotropy. By imposing an intrinsic condition on the scalar density, we derive a simplified form of the scalar field equation, which can be met under scalar field dynamics, and then, instead, we investigate scalar field frustration in the context of these theories. Furthermore, we examine, in detail, the cosmological models derived in vacuum conditions to understand the nature of isotropy and its relationship to the theory's specific characteristic, the v-vector V, which distinguishes $f(Q)$ from other teleparallel gravity models.

We initiate a study of local defining ideals of Hessenberg varieties, specifically focusing on regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A, utilizing an affine coordinate chart based on the minimal Kostant partition associated with a chosen simple root. This approach establishes a connection between geometric vertex decomposition within such varieties and the structure of local Gröbner bases, tied to a specific monomial order derived from the Euclidean distance metric. Additionally, our findings relate the local defining ideals to a specific type of partition, known as Frobenius partitions, which arise from a distinct, more general perspective of Hessenberg varieties.

Painting is a challenging, intricate process that many have struggled with for centuries. In our research, we explore generating paintings through the eyes of neural networks. Not only do our models recreate renowned artworks with astounding accuracy, but they also enable non-artistically inclined individuals to create original, high-quality paintings signed with a digital signature. This innovative technology, dubbed Neural Paint, is comprised of multiple aspects, including a brush segmentation algorithm and a style transfer system that leverages a comparison-based approach to replicate the intricate details found in brush-stroke-forged paintings. Additionally, our research involves developing a framework to assess the authenticity of paintings made using the Neural Paint method, which examines and validates the brush strokes, layer structure, and raw image features to determine a painting's neural origin. To showcase the capabilities of our technology, we demonstrated the creation of both replica and original paintings in the style of Catlin, Cezanne, and Monet, among others.

Above the TeV scale, we introduce vectorlike fields, $X$ and $\bar{X}$, that are in a bilinear combination ${\cal L}_{\text{JC}} = (X \bar{X} + \text{h.c.})$, to explore the origins of observed anomalies in $K$ and $B$ meson systems. The anomaly in the $\Delta S$ = 1 process, $\pi^0 \to \gamma \gamma$, is also addressed. Assuming the breaking of electroweak symmetry at a scale of $\sim$ TeV, the breaking of flavor symmetry, ${\cal L}_{\text{flavor breaking}} = -(\lambda_{X} \, (X \bar{X})(MD^{\dagger})^{3}) + \text{h.c.}$, causes sizable ${\pi^0}$ and ${\eta}$ decays to $\gamma \gamma$. With ${\lambda_{X}}$ within the range $2.3\leq \lambda_{X} \leq 2.8$, we can accommodate the $\pi^0$ decay width to $\gamma \gamma$ and, simultaneously, account for the observed anomalies in $K$ and $B$ mesons. The model, however, fails to explain the $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ observation. Additionally, with ${\lambda_{X}}$ in a similar range, we find that the ${

Academic researchers who read research papers usually have specific information they are trying to find - this is known as a query. Queries from researchers are often posed in an informal manner, accompanied by the title of the paper they are reading, and may include contextual details derived from the paper. We have compiled a comprehensive dataset of approximately nine thousand queries from researchers in the field of Computer Science, along with their answers. This dataset is unique because it is the only known collection of a wide range of questions related to research papers, unlike conventional knowledge bases such as Wikipedia or DBpedia. We have verified that the queries on the dataset receive accurate answers by searching through the full text of over ninety thousand research papers in the field of Computer Science, making the dataset the most accurate and comprehensive of its kind to date. This dataset is particularly useful for evaluating question answering systems, which could potentially help scientists quickly find crucial information, saving them a great deal of time.

In order to understand fast neutrino flavor instability in supernova events, we have analyzed 2- and 3-dimensional simulations. These simulations revealed neutrino instabilities primarily occur within regions where neutrinos separate and near the shockwave barrier. Notably, in a 2-dimensional model with a steeper 150 ms e-folding time, the instability remained confined to a narrower space compared to a similar model with a 200 ms e-folding time. However, in a upgraded 3-dimensional model with more accurate matter and neutrino distributions, the instability's growth rate significantly decreased by as much as 80%. We observed the instability to persist in a 3-dimensional model for an additional 100 ms beyond a comparable 2-dimensional model. These findings indicate that neutrino instabilities could survive for longer periods than previously thought.

To diagnose ADHD by analyzing resting-state fMRI data, researchers have focused on training machine learning models using the entire brain. This study makes two key contributions. First, it is established that identifying the essential regions to use is crucial for achieving high accuracy in ADHD diagnosis by reducing noise. Second, a data-driven method is created to determine the essential regions for various ADHD diagnosis algorithms and datasets. Notably, the top regions selected by this method include components linked to attention and executive functions. When the proposed method is applied to rs-fMRI data and Deep Learning algorithms, the results show significantly improved diagnostic accuracy, with benefits observed across multiple datasets and models.

In a discrete-time network where diseases spread through contact between connected nodes, our model examines an outbreak in a network where a fraction of nodes are susceptible, infected, or vaccinated. Our outbreak model builds on the discrete-time SISI model from 'A discrete-time outbreak model' by M. Feng et al., published in 2020, and extends it to a two-dimensional vector-valued system. By applying linearization techniques to a delay equation, we analyze the global asymptotic behavior of solutions and explore the impacts of delays.

MadDog is an innovative, open-source web platform designed for identifying and resolving acronyms in large texts or entire collections of texts. This versatile tool can be used for a variety of applications, such as improving the accuracy of search results by expanding acronyms, or creating customized teaching tools for students to learn about tricky acronyms in a fun and engaging way. MadDog offers a user-friendly interface for uploading texts or searches, and can be accessed through a web interface at [http://maddog.acronym.com]. Users can select from two operating methods: a pre-built frequency-based method or a custom approach using a manually constructed acronym dictionary. Additionally, MadDog provides a rich set of features for managing, visualizing, and interacting with the results of acronym identification and disambiguation processes.

Quantum interference, evident in complex quantum systems, has numerous applications in understanding natural phenomena and engineering novel devices. Recently, researchers have focused on quantum interference in electronic circuits that display unconventional correlated phenomena and exotic electron behavior. A particular electronic setup involving quantum Hall junctions shows promise for exploring quantum interference's role in generating unusual electric responses to temperature changes and heat transmission. This work examines the impact of interference in electronic paths within junctions that can switch electronically between two distinct states. By using interferometric calculations, scientists have demonstrated that, in these junctions, interference is responsible for an asymmetrical flow of heat during electronic transitions. Furthermore, this study has also discovered the possibility of using the junctions as thermoelectric switches. In addition to switching, the same electronic paths can be used for heat rectification by adjusting a relevant barrier. We have analyzed multiple junction configurations with varied barriers. Our results show that heat rectification can be achieved through electronic switches with specific properties that allow for anti-thermal behavior. This research provides a theoretical understanding of quantum interference's role in generating unique electric properties that could lead to the development of efficient thermoelectric devices and heat transmission systems.

The capacity of DNA-based data storage, with its impressive 75-to-one ratio of data to DNA molecule costs, makes it an attractive solution. To build upon this concept, we have created a data storage system that utilizes a multi-level hierarchical design, allowing for efficient compilation and efficient retrieval of data. Our innovative approach introduces a new file structure that exploits DNA's inherent properties of varying lengths and sequences to represent different levels of data hierarchy. Additionally, we have developed an algorithm to update files at lower levels in the hierarchy without disrupting higher levels, thus minimizing the impact on existing data when implementing changes. Our system is adaptable and compatible with a wide range of DNA encoding methods, allowing for flexible data encoding options. Our simulations of a DNA storage system with a capacity of 1 terabit demonstrate that our hierarchical approach reduces the complexity of data recovery from an impractical $\Omega(2^{n})$ to a more manageable $O(n)$ operation.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Various approximations have been used to describe the topology of insulators; in particular, momentum-space Wannier bands provide a simplified yet robust model to understand the underlying topology. Nodal lines in momentum space are a type of topological defect that can serve as a starting point for creating different types of nontrivial insulators. This text discusses the general importance of nodal lines in momentum space, their applications in real systems, and recent implementations in photonic and other systems.

In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to outgoing waves, which are crucial for synchronization across entire systems and are prevalent in many biological and chemical processes. These waves, which are typically triggered by pacemaker-generated activity, serve as a key mechanism to transmit information at a distance. To better understand the dynamics and scaling of these waves in complex systems, we have developed simplified analytical models to calculate their speed and efficiency in both linear and non-linear environments. Our findings, confirmed by numerical simulations, reveal that wave speed is greatest when the oscillating medium is at its furthest deviation from equilibrium, whether in a linear or non-linear capacity. Additionally, we have derived expressions for the long-term consequences of nonlinear oscillations, which are applicable to a broad range of systems beyond the scope of this study.

We investigate the quantum entropy estimation problem, aiming to find a quantum state whose density matrix is expressible as a finite sum of matrix dimensions $d$, and estimate the entropy within $h$ bits by minimizing the relative error, with both $d$ and $h$ much smaller than the total system dimension. Our research develops two novel, sublinear quantum algorithms: one can estimate entropy using $d^2\in O(1)$ quantum queries and another using $d\in O(1)$ quantum queries. Additionally, we examine the applicability of the quantum renormalization group (QRNG) method, identifying a condition under which QRNG can accurately estimate entropy in scenarios with limited access to the state.

The proliferation of artificial intelligence, a fundamental aspect of modern technology, has been facilitated by the ease of implementing AI, even for simple models, using readily available tools. Yet, for more sophisticated AI applications, particularly those utilizing deep neural networks, computational demands are significant, often necessitating the transformation of these models into highly parameterized systems. This paper sheds light on the technical underpinnings of modern AI, specifically the complexities of data storage, cloud usage, and AI pipelines, and highlights the implications of these features for AI systems. It then follows by presenting potential remedies to these issues and, in a concurrent work, presents a novel solution to these problems - a new framework for distributed AI systems that addresses these challenges through the utilization of discrete and piecewise linear functions.

Heterogeneous patient data in clinical information systems necessitate the utilization of natural language processing to facilitate automated coding for medical procedures and diagnoses. The expense and labor intricacy of manual coding, coupled with the vast quantity of clinical data, render it impractical to rely solely on traditional labeling methods. We introduce an approach, combining semi-self-supervised techniques, to enhance automatic coding efficiency. This method leverages abundant clinical notes to generate pseudo-labels for fine-tuning coding models. Notably, our approach circumvents the need for explicit model labeling during the pseudo-label generation process by first training a text representation model using a large medical corpus and then utilizing it to generate pseudo-labels based on the strength of relevant patient notes. We evaluated our approach within the context of the 2022 Infectious Disease Code (ICD) classification task and observed that our technique allowed for the utilization of longer clinical notes in contrast to traditional labels, thereby leading to a 36% decrease in labeling expense. Furthermore, our approach demonstrated improved performance in both baseline and model evaluation, achieving a 0.0484 NDCG gain over the baseline.

Let $R$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables over a field $k$. A monomial ideal $I$ within this ring is considered. This paper explores nearly Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes and provides specific classifications for certain types of ideals, including polymatroidal Veronese type and transversal polymatroidal ideals, along with illustrative examples.

Due to various practical limitations, deep neural networks typically require a considerable amount of labeled data to achieve high performance, yet obtaining enough annotated information can be challenging in numerous real-world scenarios. This difficulty is compounded by the fact that many current methods heavily rely on supervised learning techniques. In this context, we introduce two novel approaches, unsupervised quantum learning and guided quantum learning, that enable efficient use of unlabeled or partially labeled data on superconducting qubits. We test these methods on multiple datasets, including the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and a custom superconducting quantum circuit-based dataset, achieving a success rate of around 80% for the latter. Furthermore, our study indicates that combining quantum and classical techniques can lead to considerable performance gains, particularly when dealing with partially labeled data. This research represents a significant step towards the development of more data-efficient deep neural networks that are less reliant on high-quality annotated training sets.

Our team has conducted a comprehensive search through the KMTNet data system to identify planetary anomalies in 2018, focusing on prime-field objects. We developed an algorithm to remove outliers and anomalies, such as instabilities and weather events, from the dataset. Utilizing this algorithm, we were able to pinpoint 71 instances of planetary anomalies, with 31 anomalies associated with previously identified exoplanets. Our results reveal new and precise ephemerides for 13 planets, as well as an expanded period distribution analysis that suggests a median period of 6.95 days for the KMTNet dataset. Moreover, our investigation into planetary parallaxes indicates a median value of 6.895 mas for the 31 planets. With these findings, our total list of identified planetary anomalies stands at 274, comprising 122 unique exoplanets.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional numerical methods. However, existing techniques have limitations when dealing with complex scenes, particularly when it comes to accurate shadow computation.
