In particular, the most sensitive regions for detecting dark matter particles weighing sub-GeV lie within an extensive range of possible electron coupling strengths. This method can significantly aid in the investigation of dark matter particles weighing sub-GeV across an extensive range of possible electron coupling strengths. Researchers have estimated that future experiments can investigate the majority of the parameter space for which the direct-detection method has an enhanced sensitivity compared to the conventional method that involves directly recording nuclear recoils.

This paper examines the behavior of a two-level atom interacting with a quantum cavity under both weak and strong light, similar to the Jaynes-Cummings model, but with key differences. Specifically, the paper focuses on a context where the cavity is in a superposition of excited and unexcited states at t=0, as opposed to being in a definite state. This distinction gives rise to a model known as the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model. The study reveals the non-equivalence of this model and the Jaynes-Cummings model in terms of particle transmission and the formation of entangled states. Furthermore, the paper analyzes the phenomenon of Rabi oscillations and identifies a unique condition under which the two-level atom and the cavity display synchronized motion. Moreover, the paper demonstrates that in the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, there is a unique transmission pattern of photons compared to the Jaynes-Cummings model. However, the paper also notes that in both models, entangled states are created through a quantum transmission process. Additionally, the paper differentiates the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model from a qubit-cavity system where a single photon interacts with a qubit.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have involved the use of deep learning, which has significantly improved signal quality and diagnostic accuracy, far exceeding previous limitations. A novel deep learning approach is being developed using a Tiramisu autoencoder to effectively filter out motion artifact and make ECG signals more interpretable even during high-impact motion. By achieving accurate denoising and IBI estimation, this approach accelerates diagnostic processes and achieves better results. Notably, our technique has successfully estimated IBIs from ECG signals with signal-to-noise ratios of up to -30 decibels and achieved average root mean square error of 13 milliseconds. This level of accuracy surpasses existing benchmarks.

We use Onsager variational methods to analyze active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles, which are particles governed by a force that depends on their position, velocity, and a set of interaction rules that encourage them to move towards favorable locations. Our study focuses on the average work done by these forces as they direct other particles towards more beneficial areas. By introducing a set of variables and a corresponding functional, we are able to derive compact mathematical representations of the average work under two different scenarios - either all particles are actively guided or only some are actively guided. For situations where all particles are actively involved, we derive a formula for the average work and demonstrate that it can be expressed as a product of two factors, each of which is unaffected by the system's non-linear characteristics. For cases where only some particles are actively involved, we demonstrate that the average work can be expressed as a product of two factors - the probability of a particle reaching a certain location and a force that depends only on the location and velocity of the particle, and a set of interaction rules that encourage them to move towards favorable locations. Our study confirms that the average work can be expressed as a product of two factors - the probability of a particle reaching a certain location and a force that depends only on the system's non-linear characteristics.

The capture of human movement through multiple viewpoints is crucial for developing comprehensive gesture recognition systems. To address this, we introduce HUMBI, a large-scale dataset featuring multiple views of human body gestures, owned by one individual. This record includes a diverse range of gestures, captured from five different viewpoints, along with a variety of superimposed poses that mimic real-world clothing and accessories. Current pose estimation methods fall short when handling occlusion, a significant drawback. To overcome this, we developed HMNet, a novel multi-view system that can handle and recover from occluded poses. As an alternative, we introduced a novel, view-agnostic representation method that does not rely on complex camera positioning data. Based on this, we crafted HMRecon, a view-agnostic pose recovery method. To evaluate these methods, we established the HUMBI Challenge, an important benchmark for the community. On two separate tasks, HMRecon emerged as the top performer, surpassing leading benchmarks. This code and dataset will be made publicly available.

Many researchers agree that incorporating knowledge of task classification can enhance cross-lingual transfer in neural models. Nevertheless, labeling each task with a specific class can be labor-intensive. To mitigate this issue, our approach utilizes class labels solely to establish a similarity metric between tasks, thereby providing a weak guidance system for our method. We developed a new cross-lingual training protocol, which utilizes a dual approach. Firstly, it generates task embeddings from both language-agnostic class labels and language-specific sentence representations. Secondly, it fine-tunes these task embeddings while adjusting sentence embeddings to maximize cross-lingual transfer. We evaluated our method on two datasets, achieving a substantial gain in classification accuracy across both single-task and multi-task settings. Notably, our approach demonstrated a considerable advantage in scenarios with limited training data.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our study, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across video frames. Our improved model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable enhancement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, BasicVSR++ exhibits impressive generalization to diverse video sequences, as evident from our thorough benchmark tests.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, solving one task can hinder progress on another task, a issue known as catastrophic interference. We've found that in reinforcement learning, a module-based approach can successfully avoid this problem when applied to other people's tasks. By using pre-trained modules from the DeepMind Control Suite, a collection of control tasks, we've demonstrated the ability to learn new tasks without losing previously learned ones. Furthermore, this approach leads to faster training overall. We've also discovered that when there's no natural difference between tasks, using a single module for all of them, a method known as shared reinforcement learning, actually increases the risk of catastrophic interference, although not entirely eliminate it. By contrast, module-based approaches that tailor each task to its own custom module are most effective at avoiding this problem, but require more training data.

We have improved the performance of thermal machines operating within specific timeframes by accounting for the limitations of the controller. The overhaul involves introducing a new measure of efficiency that's directly related to the operator constraints, thereby providing a feasible solution for a critical optimization problem. The novel efficiency measure serves as a lower bound for the conventional efficiency measure in finite-time scenarios. Additionally, we have developed a method to determine the operational point at which the maximum efficiency occurs. The methods developed can be applied broadly to work with various types of operator constraints. The results are validated by applying them to a previously studied heat engine operating within specific timeframes and controlled by two different sets of limits, resulting in significant improvements in performance when compared to traditional approaches that ignore controller limitations.

This research explores the effect of spatially co-occurring hurricanes and storm surges on power systems in the Gulf Coast of the United States. Through an analysis of 18 major hurricanes that hit the region between 1938 and 2012, we quantify the impact of assaultive storms on Oklahoma's power grid, discovering that they can cause multiple grid failures in the process. Furthermore, we develop an analytical framework to assess these catastrophic events, which we apply to the ISO New England power grid, identifying potential hurricane and storm surge threats. Our study ultimately recommends developing more sophisticated models for evaluating multiplicative threat scenarios, which could lead to groundbreaking failure prevention strategies, giving utilities a competitive advantage, and providing essential input for grid resilience planning.

This article explores a significant conjecture known as the three balls conjecture within the context of Clifford analysis. It focuses specifically on eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator, which are subject to certain linear independence constraints. The article building blocks are the fundamental solutions to the Dirac operator, which are discussed in detail, along with their relevant properties. The main part of the article establishes the proof of the conjecture for even-dimensional spaces, while a related theorem is proven for odd-dimensional spaces.

We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. The representation of these maps in matrix form facilitates their study through linear algebra techniques, allowing us to identify 3D analogs of the Dyck system and establish a relationship between them. While both the 2D baker map and their 3D counterparts exhibit entropy-maximizing properties when applied to Lebesgue measure, the transition to other measures reveals a mechanism for the breakdown of entropy accessibility, providing a mathematical explanation for the phenomenon observed in the stability analysis of the generalized baker maps.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the scalar boson with a 125 GeV mass by the LHC, a broad range of potential scalar multiplicity theories has been developed where additional, heavier scalars may exist. Researchers have explored the prospects of discovering these additional scalars through multiple observational methods including direct production, indirect production via gauge boson loops, and through the investigation of scalar decay patterns, particularly in the cases of $\bar{b} \bar{b} \gamma$ and $\bar{\tau} \bar{\tau} \gamma$. Future high-energy colliders such as the LHC upgrade, HL-LHC, ILC, CLIC, and FCC-hh are expected to play a crucial role in the ongoing search for these additional scalars as they offer the capability of precise scalar coupling measurements necessary for a thorough understanding of the expanded scalar sectors. In this article, we will review the theoretical frameworks of these expanded scalar models and the potential discoveries as well as measurements of their properties using the capabilities of future high-energy colliders.

This paper introduces quasi-periodic WaveNet, an advanced generative model based on WaveNet architecture. To enhance the latter's capabilities, quasi-periodic WaveNet incorporates a pitch-dependent expanded convolution neural network into its autoregressive framework. This innovative model leverages the strengths of both WaveNet and convolutional networks to effectively model raw audio signals. As a result, it delivers high-quality speech synthesis at a previously unachievable scale, while consuming relatively fewer computational resources. To validate its effectiveness, synthesis demonstrations and a qualitative comparison with WaveNet and other generative models will be presented. Moreover, a series of listening tests will be conducted to assess the performance of quasi-periodic WaveNet.

To tackle the inherent biases and subjectivity in user preferences, this study advocates for a bicluster-based approach in recommendation systems. The proposed method involves creating pairs of user and item clusters, where users sharing similar preferences are grouped together with respect to the items they engage with. It also incorporates several objective functions to optimize the entanglement of users and items in the bicluster-based framework. The results of extensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the suggested framework and its variants in outperforming state-of-the-art recommender systems.

The schedule for the HARPS-N solar telescope over the next decade includes observing the Sun with a spectrometer that has a resolution of 115,000, which will provide important data for studying the Sun's magnetic cycles and behavior. The Sun's intense magnetic fields cause chemical shifts in light that can be used to determine the Sun's movement across the face of the Sun and its magnetic properties. However, these shifts are also affected by other processes, like the Sun's rotation and the motion of gas across the Sun's face, which need to be accounted for in the analysis. The current study used the Sun's rotation and gas flow patterns to improve the simulation of the Sun's spectral observations, which are essential for understanding the Sun's magnetic cycles through harp-like data. Some new activity indicators were developed using this corrected model and tested against previous observations of the Sun by the SOT/Hinode and IRIS/IFU telescopes. The results of these tests suggest that the new indicators are able to detect the Sun's magnetic cycles as well as established processes. The corrected model and new indicators are important for understanding the Sun's magnetic cycles in detail, which will be observed by the HARPS-N solar telescope in the coming years.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves analyzing the temperature dependence of these peaks through resistance measurements. The use of high resistance electrodes in the setup ensures Ohmic dissipation, making it possible to verify whether the original assumption holds. If not, the response can provide insight into the local density of states near the non-Majorana zero-energy levels. Furthermore, our method enables the normalisation of tunneling conductance data by taking into account both the resistance and the local density of states. In addition, we demonstrate that Majorana-related conductance fluctuations below the non-injecting electrode's non-Majorana zero-energy level can serve as an alternative method for Majorana identification. These ideas are explained using an analytical model based on a numerical model that was previously developed.

Mark Kaminski initially introduced Bicategories of Shadows as a way to extend the concepts of shadow and fractal for complex data sets in higher dimensions. This paper provides a detailed interpretation of Bicategories of Shadows, demonstrating that they represent a distinctive category of bicategories that maintain key characteristics of the original Bicategories of Shadows. The investigation also establishes connections between features of these bicategories and fundamental properties of the underlying categories of shadows. It is observed that bicategories of shadows exhibit a strong association with weakly decomposable categories, which have the potential to be simple or complex. The relationship between bicategories of shadows and marks on categories has also been discovered, with marks serving as an essential tool for analyzing category properties. This research builds on existing research by Mike Shulman to link marks to strict marks, with bicategories of shadows now acting as a bridge between these concepts. The study concludes by exploring potential applications of bicategories of shadows in the study of complex data sets in higher dimensions.

A current technique, style transfer, allows one image to be transformed into the style of another, though it tends to put more emphasis on the aesthetic qualities of the resulting transformation. In the case of adjusting skin tone to match a desired curve, the output can also appear unnatural or exaggerated. To address this, a new approach, global hue mapping, is developed to accurately transfer an image's hue based on a desired curve. It is complemented by an inverse method to restore the original image from a warped one with adjusted hue. Both methods are efficient, being scalable with the square of the number of color channels, and are demonstrated to produce more subtle results on skin tone adjustment. To capture the desired tone from an image, a multi-scale dilated convolutional network is used, and the resulting tone is then applied to the global hue mapping method through a new distillation process, achieving more natural results. Testing on both general hue mapping and skin tone adjustment indicates the new approach outperforms the conventional method in reducing artifacts. The source code for replicating the results in the paper can be found on the https://github.com/JayMyer/ghm repository.

This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC task, recently introduced in the LOVEU challenge at CVPR 2022, where experts faced significant challenges in processing multi-step responses, multiple modalities, and dynamic button representations within video content. To overcome this, we developed a novel context-grounding module that enhances feature mapping using attention mechanisms. We further explored the effects of varying button counts, conducted ablation studies on different network architectures and video feature types, and attained a 2nd place ranking overall in the LOVEU track 3 competition. Notably, we achieved a 1st place ranking in two of the four evaluation metrics. Our open-source code is accessible via the repository link at https://github.com/jaykim9870/CVPR-22_LOVEU_unipyler.

In snowstorms, atmospheric turbulence causes snow particles to move randomly, but their fall is also influenced by their size, leading to complex patterns of accumulation. To understand how smaller particles overcome obstacles created by larger ones, researchers studied snowfall using a unique facility that generates controlled turbulence. By analyzing the structure of developing snow layers, they discovered evidence of a process called selective sweeping, where larger particles alter the turbulence environment, causing smaller particles to be dropped at a lower rate. This process leads to an unusual distribution of particle sizes in the snow layer, with thicker layers often containing fewer larger particles than thinner layers. This phenomenon has been observed in both the laboratory and nature, and its implications could also be applied to other fields, such as biology and geology, where similar particle sorting phenomena may occur.

As robots interact with their environment, their decisions have direct consequences,
resulting in inherent linkages between their actions and subsequent observations.
This intrinsic connection is often overlooked in the application of active learning
techniques to robot learning, where predictions are commonly based on past data.
We propose a novel approach, integrating a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method with
real-time decision-making, to leverage the robot's dynamic trajectory and sense
first-hand data for active prediction purposes.
By adopting a probabilistic perspective, we reframe past performances as incomplete
data and predict future outcomes as the expected value of their distribution.
Given limited time, the robot prioritizes the most predictive new measurements to
update its forecast, breaking the barrier between past and future performance with
improved generalization capabilities.
Experimental evaluations on a quadcopter and a wheeled robot demonstrate up to
40% better prediction outcomes compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

In the field of particle physics, researchers need to process massive amounts of data produced by sub-atomic particle detectors. This paper focuses on addressing the data reduction challenge in Three-Dimensional Sparse TPC, a specific type of particle detector used in the J-PET project. To achieve this, researchers propose a novel, deep-learning approach, utilizing a unified autoencoder that employs Bicephalous networks. By treating data reduction as a data compression task, the autoencoder is trained to minimize data loss while reducing dimensions. The authors showcase the feasibility and efficiency of this method in reducing data as-needed, and highlight its potential for automatic feature extraction, thus increasing the'search' dimension of the search space. The study utilizes a sparse dataset derived from Cosmic events recorded by the JetPET detector.

Utilizing the Finzi gravity theory, which treats the Newtonian constant $G_N$ as a dynamically generated variable, our research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of galaxy clusters. We observe that the radial distribution of mass within these clusters follows a Rosseaux law, which is analogous to the isothermal distribution seen in thermodynamics. We construct a thermodynamic chart for galaxy clusters and identify that the entropy of these clusters is connected to the radial velocity of particles, while the entropy density is connected to the radial distribution of mass. We obtain a universal equation for thermodynamic potential, which aligns with the findings from thermodynamics. We also investigate how Finzi gravity affects the mass profiles and thermal energies of galaxy clusters. We discover that by adjusting $G_N$, the structure of these clusters can be modified. We establish a relationship between temperature and radial distance, which is characterized by a $G_N$-dependent coefficient. We calculate the thermal energy of these clusters as a function of the virial radius and find that their temperatures follow a $G_N$-dependent trend. We make a prediction that based on the strong coupling of gravity, the temperature of these clusters will decrease as they form. We assume that the gravitational potential in these clusters is dominated by a central mass, which allows us to model the thermal behavior of these clusters using the Finzi gravity model. We demonstrate that our findings from numerical investigations can be replicated through an analytical approach by solving the equations of hydrodynamics in the context

In this research, we examine a phenomenon known as saturation in convex geometric hypergraphs, specifically focusing on its applications to the problems of extremal combinatorics. This work is a continuation of previous studies by Garban, Mason, and Peters on standard hypergraphs. Here, we're investigating a specific class of convex geometric hypergraphs where the vertices are points in the plane and the maximal subsets have a collective area within a given threshold. This geometric constraint serves as the basis for a new theorem that addresses the maximum number of such geometric hypergraphs with a given size. This research is further illustrated by deriving specific results for the maximum sizes of geometric hypergraphs with specific properties. This paper is a continuation of the previous studies by Garban, Mason, and Peters on standard hypergraphs. Here, we're investigating a phenomenon that reflects a geometric representation of the Erdos-Szemeredi theorem. This research is further illustrated by applying the obtained results to a problem that involves the covering of the plane by triangles. This problem is a geometric representation of the Sunflower conjecture, where the vertices of the triangles are colored with at least three distinct colors.

To understand how to form p-rich isotopes through the $^{6}$Li+$^{51}$V nuclear reaction, researchers have investigated how inclusive $\alpha$ cross-sections are affected by the relative orientations of $\alpha$ and core fragments. Computer simulations, utilizing the APMC code and incorporating a mean-field potential, were conducted to analyze how the directional distribution of $\alpha$ particles impacts their overall cross-section. This study's aim is to provide a foundation for studying the nuclear reaction mechanisms that produce p-rich isotopes through the $^{6}$Li+$^{51}$V reaction, which is significant for materials analysis in nuclear applications.

A novel and resource-efficient approach to locomotion is exhibited by the Pacific lamprey, a fish that uses a unique gait to move up aquatic slopes with minimal energy expenditure. This paper outlines the development of a robotic system inspired by the Pacific lamprey's propulsion mechanism, designed to transit through tight spaces with reduced frictional losses. The described system comprises a compact, lightweight construction that integrates adjustable fins and a central tail to produce an anti-parabolic trajectory of the tail blade, facilitating efficient propulsion. In addition to the descriptive components, this paper presents a theoretical framework for understanding the relationships between system parameters, input signals, and resulting forces. To validate the described technology, a test rig was used to measure the performance of the Pacific lamprey-inspired robot when transiting through narrow channels, comparing its climbing capabilities to a state-of-the-art robot. The developed system demonstrated superior performance, with reduced energy losses and increased climbing speeds.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework for modeling colon cancer treatment responses in individuals with different health profiles. It utilizes the Fokker-Planck equation to derive probabilistic distributions based on treatment impacts, which are then optimized through a suitable objective function. We employ a finite difference method to numerically simulate the probabilistic distributions of cancer progression and immune response in each patient. Our results indicate that an optimal treatment regimen can be identified through multiple simultaneous interventions, which maximize the patient's quality of life while minimizing severe side effects. The proposed approach has been validated by comparing its outputs with those of existing modeling methods for colon cancer treatment, revealing excellent agreement. A notable feature of this framework is its ability to generate personalized treatment recommendations for patients with similar health conditions by analyzing their individual probabilistic distributions of cancer progression and immune response.

Optimizing system performance in D2D systems has been a major D2D research focus. Traditionally, this optimization has centered on maximizing network capabilities such as capacity and coverage. This work diverges from this approach by exploring direct optimization of the Age of Information (AoI), a measure of data freshness. Introducing a deep neural network to compute the best D2D pairing configuration, the research shows that this approach is both efficient and scalable. After the network selects the optimal pairings in each TTI, a resource allocation algorithm ensures the selected devices can establish communication while maximizing their spatial frequency reuse. This novel two-phase optimization method achieves superior results in both low and high traffic scenarios, surpassing alternatives and providing a clear path forward for implementations.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [27] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic flow. This current work examines helicity in a more complex scenario - compressible flow with no viscosity and barotropic density. To do this, we define "conservation law density" and "helicity density", deriving their vector fields from specific properties of the fluid's internal energy. By establishing that these densities along with their corresponding gradient lie on the same parallel in a specific Lie algebra, we prove the non-conservation of helicity in the case of smooth solutions to the compressible Euler equations, assuming that the fluid does not contain any rotational motion. On the other hand, we prove the conservation of helicity in the case of the fluid being strictly hyperbolic critical points without any rotation.

The researchers in a particular study demonstrated that in an explicitly defined two-component Bose-Einstein condensate model, a specific type of instability occurs when linearly propagating interfaces are presented. Furthermore, it was found that a significant increase in reflection occurs at certain limits of wave number. By applying a new approach, it was possible to explain this phenomenon. Utilizing this approach, it was determined that a significant maximum in reflection exists at a specific limit of wave number. Using numerical simulations, it was confirmed that this maximum occurs in regions where a particular type of instability is present in the system.

A strong possibility exists that the upcoming advanced x-ray lasers will reach the limits of our current understanding in the Seabas criterion. The possibility of generating highly coherent x-ray pulses could lead to major breakthroughs in scientific research. In this study, we explore the potential of leveraging the capabilities of a free-electron laser oscillator by utilizing it as the seed for driving a free-electron laser to produce high-intensity, highly coherent x-ray pulses. The feasibility of achieving high-intensity x-ray pulses was demonstrated through numerical simulations, which showed that increasing the number of pulses from the oscillator can significantly boost the energy and peak power of the x-ray pulses. The simulation results indicate that it is plausible to achieve x-ray pulses with high energy (on the order of tens of joules), high peak power (reaching levels of tens of gigawatts), and low coherence (on the order of a few percent), which makes such pulses highly beneficial for a wide range of scientific applications.

Transportation networks are an ideal example of dynamic graphs where traffic patterns are expected to conform to certain norms but can deviate from them due to unexpected incidents such as vehicle accidents, natural disasters, or system failures. The primary goal of incident detection in this context is to identify anomalous instances on the graph edges that differentiate from regular traffic. This research aims to solve this problem by first defining incident-free traffic using historical node normalisation techniques and then identifying anomalies through subsequent detection. A node anomaly score is calculated to identify abnormal activity, which is then used to construct an adaptive threshold model for real-time incident detection. The proposed method is rigorous and has been mathematically proven to be accurate and reliable, with results from traffic graph datasets demonstrating its effectiveness.

This study examines self-similar solutions to the fluid dynamics equations near a point where there is a sudden increase in density within a medium. It starts with a basic model in which the fluid is accelerating towards this point under the influence of gravity or an attractive force. We are looking for solutions that describe how the fluid behaves just before it reaches the point of highest density, where the pressure becomes maximally concentrated. In this model, the fluid can be considered as having a single flow direction, simplifying it to a one-dimensional problem. We are interested in self-similar solutions that remain descriptive throughout the implosion process. Such solutions are known to be a part of a broader class of solutions that are relevant in a wider range of scenarios. In this context, we are looking for solutions with a specific asymptotic behavior but are also considering the possibility of other self-similar solutions with different asymptotics. It is possible that multiple solutions with different properties will be relevant in this model.

The growing demand for Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems in private and public sectors may lead to significant financial gains, but it also raises important ethical concerns that must be addressed. The central issue surrounding many AI systems is the lack of transparency and clarity in their decisions, which has resulted in a significant number of users rejecting AI-powered solutions. The field of Explainable AI aims to make AI systems more understandable to humans, but current approaches often focus on improving machine learning models without considering users' needs. This paper proposes a new approach that incorporates the principles of Requirements Engineering to identify the specific understandable requirements for each AI system, based on the characteristics of its users. By centering AI development around user requirements, we can create more transparent and trustworthy AI systems that better align with users' interests. The proposed method demonstrates its effectiveness in analyzing a real-world AI system and identifies key understandable requirements that can improve user engagement and loyalty.

This research paper presents UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset of colorectal polyp samples derived from 482 histopathology specimens captured through whole-slide imaging. The dataset includes histopathology reports to facilitate reliable clinical diagnosis. The abstract also outlines the process of the dataset's creation, its comprehensive information, and the findings of initial validation experiments for both classification and evaluation of adenoma grading. The dataset is divided into three parts: a training set with 320 samples, a test set with 81 specimens, and a separate category for validation and comparison purposes. Due to technical limitations, the original paper could only demonstrate the effectiveness of uniToPatho in classifying benign and malignant lesions. As such, the training and test sets only encompass samples with benign, adenomatous, or malignant characteristics. For more detailed information regarding the dataset's construction, classification experiments, and grading assessment, the respective Methodology, Classification Task, and Grading Task sections are referenced.

A well-known incident in 2019, referred to as the 'Hotel Mars', demonstrated how hotel guests had access to IEEE conference talks, including one by Anil Adriaisey, through public discussions at breakfast. This incident highlights the potential for data leakage in systems designed for information sharing. Within this context, we examine the problem of minimizing data leakage from a sender to a receiver given a confidential library of exponentials and an public realm with restricted access. Our analysis of data leakage in zero-error source coding reveals the important distinction between k-tuple and individual data leakage. This distinction is further illustrated through the creation of a graph representing the confidential library, where vertices correspond to distinct letters from this library. An edge exists between two vertices if the letters they represent can not be used together in a valid exponential. This graph, referred to as the Incompatible Graph, is shown to be perfect if it is k-tuple non-trivial but perfect. This work also presents an algorithm for determining the k-tuple data leakage capacity, or rather the k-tuple non-trivial data leakage capacity, by utilizing a maximum flow algorithm in the Incompatible Graph. This algorithm seeks to maximize the flow from the sender to the receiver given a confidential library of exponentials and an public realm with restricted access. It is noted but not proven that this algorithm may approach the optimal data leakage capacity, or rather the optimal k-tuple non-trivial data leakage capacity, when the Incompatible Graph is k-tuple non

We introduce MrSARP, a novel deep generative model based on hierarchical low-rank representations, to improve the quality of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images. SAR images face degradation due to factors like speckle noise, interferometric phase noise, and data losses during transmission, rendering them unusable for various applications. Existing denoising methods are largely adaptation-specific, requiring adjusted parameters for different scenarios, which proves impractical. Our proposed MrSARP model leverages a stack-based low-rank representation to generate SAR images, thus learning a prior that is inherently embedded within the system. Built upon a stack-based autoencoder with skip connections, MrSARP incorporates two hierarchical encoders to extract low-rank features from radar data. The learned priors are then used to derive an optimal solution for SAR image enhancement through a convex optimization technique. MrSARP shows remarkable performance on various types of SAR images, outshining several leading methods, including internal filter-based approaches and external deep learning techniques. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/Qianhui-Yu/MrSARP.

No optimization method is superior to all others in every scenario, which is why research aims to uncover when Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm's variant can surpass classical competitors. To address this, our approach introduces a Bayesian tuning technique to optimize QAOA parameters and thus enhances its performance. The suggested method involves treating parameter selection as a hyperparameter search problem and utilizing a Bayesian process to gather information from related experiments. This process allows for predicting likely outcomes based on observed results and guiding subsequent investigations. The Bayesian approach then employs a utility function to identify the optimal parameter setting for a specific problem, which has been demonstrated in various experiments to be effective in finding suitable parameters compared to cross-validation in various scenarios. Moreover, our findings show that integrating the Bayesian approach into QAOA results in a significant improvement in solution quality on specific problems and a comparable or superior outcome on others, especially when facing situations with limited resources constraint.

In various geometric applications, determining the area of an ellipse is a pressing issue. For instance, in the field of semiconductor manufacturing, calculating overlap between circular objects is crucial. Unfortunately, exact matching of elliptical shapes is a complex problem, making direct calculation of their overlap area challenging. However, this problem can be tackled by utilizing elliptical cross-sections of 3D shapes, which facilitates the implementation of an efficient algorithm. The proposed method employs a novel approach based on dividing the area into simpler regions and using elliptic integrals to achieve a high degree of precision. While this basic concept is straightforward, achieving significant computational performance required an in-depth analysis of the underlying mathematics. The resulting algorithm integrates accurately calculated areas of overlapping elliptical regions a priority, which proves beneficial in the context of computational geometry.

Employing continuous time for decision-making processes can yield more
realistic outcomes by eliminating the artificial constraints associated with
discrete time models. Despite this, continuous-duration reinforcement learning
remains an underdeveloped field of study. We present a novel approach by
integrating Q-learning with continuous time to form Continuous Duration
Q-learning (CDQ). This method allows for the learning of optimal policies in
environments with variable episode lengths. Building on the concept of
intermediate rewards, CDQ extends Q-learning to continuous time by representing
the reward function as a capability map. This map initially estimates the
potential reward a agent can achieve within a certain time frame. As the
agent interacts with the environment, the capability map evolves, and the
agent's objective is to maximize this map. Since traditional Q-learning methods
are based on the assumption that states are discrete and non-parametric, we
develop a new method to apply Q-learning to continuous states using a capability
map as a parameterized representation. Moreover, CDQ learning is built on the
 assumption of bounded differences (BDD) to ensure the stability of the
algorithm. We tested CDQ in various scenarios, including a task-oriented
dialogue system, and demonstrated its capability to learn optimal policies in
environments with variable episode lengths.

Quantum magnets' dynamical structure factor is a critical measurement, but making predictions for multi-dimensional models like Hubbard is complicated due to computational and theoretical constraints. We investigated magnetic excitations in a 2D triangular-lattice Hubbard model with up to 10 x 10 sites, using the flexible 2D lattice scaling method. Our results for the antiferromagnetic phase agree with earlier research and demonstrate a partial order-by-disorder effect, where quantum fluctuations favor 120-degree spin ordering. Additionally, we discovered that spin waves become more stable as the system becomes more correlated, a phenomenon also found in other triangular-lattice models. We also mapped the phase diagram of the model and examined the interplay between magnetic, metabolic, and superconducting phases, as well as the role of stripe ordering. Our research provides a comprehensive picture of magnetic behaviors in the model and sheds light on the origins of 120-degree and stripe ordering.

Vertebral location and identification are crucial processes in spinal pathology analysis. However, pinpointing their exact position in three-dimensional CT scans while accounting for natural spine curvature and varying vertebral sizes presents a significant challenge. Many existing methods rely on straightforward sectioning or voxelation, but these often overlook the intricate relationships between nearby vertices and opt for a straightforward'slice-and-replace' approach. By contrast, a more sophisticated technique uses a spine alignment template to ensure accurate vertebral positioning throughout the CT volume. But even with advanced optimization, the resulting method struggles with variability, particularly when dealing with thoracic and lumbar vertebrae. Building on this foundation, we introduce an advanced technique that uses vertebral size and curvature constraints to refine optimization and achieve better results. The new method surpasses state-of-the-art performance, as evidenced by successful validation on two public datasets and impressive results in two related tasks. The code for this research method can be freely accessed at the provided URL.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes in physical systems, making it an effective framework for analyzing irreversible processes from a thermodynamic perspective. Similar to electrical currents in circuit theory, the flow of energy through thermodynamic systems is described using discrete jump processes. This work uses purely mathematical methods to investigate the statistical properties of system currents based on simulated data. We initially establish the mathematical underpinnings of these currents, then derive and justify formulas for calculating statistical measures, such as the average power from digital simulation data. We argue that the primary method for evaluating these measures is the frequency approach. Importantly, we formally prove that the frequency method is unaffected by a specific type of digital simulation artifacts, ensuring its validity and reliability. Under certain conditions, the linear regression method can be used to calculate limiting statistics, and we explain the equivalence between this approach and the frequency method. We also identify two types of digital simulation experiments that validate the frequency method's efficiency in calculating limiting statistics, and demonstrate that the influence of artificial uncertainties in these experiments vanishes in the relevant limiting cases.

This work extends the relative quantum field theory, originally an analysis of local relations on symplectic resolutions, to more complex geometric settings, specifically on log canonical singularities with various equivalent models. It demonstrates that the relative correlation functions on specific models share a common limit within a suitable scaling limit. To achieve this, it proves that the equivalent models share key properties of the relative field theory. The resulting quantum field theory is characterized by a highly invariant structure, where the relative correlation functions are entirely determined by their behavior on specific models, regardless of the chosen representation.

Theoretical and experimental investigations have shown that there is total
transmission of acoustic waves between closely spaced piezoelectric materials.
This phenomenon occurs due to the conversion of longitudinal waves into
perpendicular polarized transverse waves at the material interface. A
reflection-free interface condition is established by matching acoustic wave
properties, leading to the emergence of a specific type of wave known as a
surface wave that doesn't change direction and remains confined to the material
surface. This results in the conversion of a portion of the original longitudinal
wave into a transverse wave. A detailed analysis of the piezoelectric materials'
crystal structure and symmetry is conducted to determine the allowed wave modes
at the material interface. A significant finding is that when the wave modes on both
sides of the interface coincide, there is total transmission of acoustic waves.
Otherwise, there is total transmission of the longitudinal wave and partial
transmission of the transverse wave. This theory is verified using experiments
with closely spaced piezoelectric materials, such as lithium niobate and
gallium pyrochlore.

We explore the use of exciton-polariton condensates in microcavities as a novel class of nonlinear light sources within a photonic integrated circuit platform. The interaction between the polariton condensate and the microcavity modes enables the transmission of non-trivial light signals, facilitating study of complex photonics through wave propagation in integrated circuits. Our research delves into the digital transmission capabilities of the polariton condensate, while also investigating the influence of spatial structure and phase instability on the polariton condensate, which can lead to phase-stepped transmission in integrated circuits. We develop a theoretical model to explain these observations and outline a prospective approach to mitigate phase instability, thereby enhancing the digital transmission performance. This research has the potential to contribute to the development of more sophisticated integrated photonics with adjustable optical properties at the heart of a photonic circuit.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process of this debris still unknown. Analyzing grain size and sublimation rate is essential in comprehending the environment that contributes to planetary disintegration. In this study, dual-band photometry obtained through the Large Binocular Telescope enabled us to distinguish between two grain populations, confirming earlier observations of smaller particles and discovering evidence of larger particles, approximately 0.5 to 1 micron in size. By modeling both populations simultaneously, we determined dust loss rates, with the required mass loss rate for K2-22b exceeding earlier estimates, approximately 3.6 * 10^8 grams per second. These results may implicate a different scenario for the planetary disintegration, with the possibility that the destroyed planet lies within the temperate zone of its host star gaining less support. These findings also recommend targeting this exoplanet in future studies using the James Webb Space Telescope and other instruments that can probe various wavelength ranges.

We establish a novel condition that must be satisfied by the components of a complex variety's Milnor fiber. This condition is tied to the flatness of the variety's critical locus, and from it, we derive previously unknown consequences of singularities in codimension two or higher. For instance, when the variety's local fundamental locus coincides with its critical locus, we show that its Milnor fiber segments exhibit coherence. This result extends the coherence theorem for nodal singularities, previously proven by Lê, Nguyen, and Ta, to include singularities of higher codimension.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform library designed for interactive data analysis and.NET-powered computing. Developed using C# and.NET Standard 2.0, Daany is highly adaptable and can be used in various environments, including Windows, Linux, and macOS. It's particularly suitable for data analysts and data scientists working with Microsoft technologies, offering a versatile alternative to Python-based data analysis tools. Daany is centered around data frames, providing users with easy-access calculators, data manipulation tools, and statistics functionalities. The library also focuses on machine learning, including regression and classification algorithms, as well as time series analysis and optimization techniques. Daany's comprehensive API enables seamless integration with other.NET libraries, facilitating efficient data analysis tasks.

I challenge the conventional view that there was a seamless, unbroken thread connecting ancient Greek intellectual traditions to the foundational knowledge of the scientific revolution. Instead, I contend that the revolution marked a significant turning point in the history of science. To support this claim, I'll examine key aspects of Galileo's methodology, highlighting his reliance on mathematical rather than purely theoretical approaches. This analysis will be followed by an exploration of the implications of the Ignoramus verdict delivered by Cardinal McLean's tribunal in 1632.

The universe's early stages transitioned from a completely dark and matter-dominated state at a temperature of $\sim 0.1$ MeV to a radiant, energy-dominated state at $\sim 0.1$ MeV, marking the universe's earliest significant change. The reorganization was achieved through the massive liberation of photons as electrons and protons became nucleons, a process described by Saha's ionization equation. The equilibrium was reached nearly 400,000 years after the universe's inception, an era marked by the cosmos's earliest significant change.

In a study of this reorganization, researchers have found that the influences of ionization follow a non-Gaussian, asymmetrical pattern. The reorganization underwent a period of significant growth right before reaching equilibrium, characterized by an unusual, asymmetrical shape, often referred to as a "plateau then spike." This distinctive feature is a result of considering only a single type of nucleon for the reorganization, a limitation which significantly affects the non-Gaussian influences, causing them to vary greatly from one scenario to another. The reorganization's non-Gaussian characteristics have implications for understanding cosmic structure development using the primordial spectrum, a phenomenon which may provide further insights into the cosmos's initial conditions.

The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex particle-in-cell simulations that are often beyond the scope of current computational capabilities. Typically, such simulations are reserved for specific, in-depth studies, whereas more general research relies on less complex simulations involving fluid-based models. In an effort to bridge this gap, we have developed a new adaptiveIMPACT model that can be utilized in global simulations with varying levels of complexity. This impact model embeds an implicitly resolved, fully kinetic particle-in-cell interior within a global magnetohydrodynamics framework, allowing for seamless integration. By embedding the IMPACT model within a 3D MHD simulation, we have performed a general study on magnetic island coalescence and have obtained results comparable to those of conventional PIC simulations. The Adaptively Embedded IMPACT model has efficiently addressed the challenge of modeling magnetic reconnection on an openly accessible, global scale while achieving computational savings of up to two orders of magnitude.

This research introduces Amanuensis, an innovative collaborative learning platform designed to prepare human programmers-in-training with the assistance of machine-learning-trained 'aidants'. Amanuensis is built on a principle of mutual learning where its algorithms learn from the insights gained during co-learning between humans and machines. Developed from a combination of conceptual foundations in organizational theory, learning theories, and proven methods from multi-agent systems, Amanuensis is demonstrated to facilitate effective learning through statistical analysis. To ensure smooth learning processes, the system is equipped with tools like learning pace management, performance assessment, and feedback adjustment. Our study compares the performance of Amanuensis against alternative approaches, revealing that it significantly reduces the duration required for human programmers-in-training to achieve the same level of proficiency.
